champion.partB: Double-jeopardy/multiple-punishments claim preserved at Vol. 4 pp. 4–6 and re-urged at pp. 92–97; the court deferred ruling ('We can cover it later'), then denied at p. 97 on a Blockburger 'contact versus penetration' rationale. Under Patterson v. State, 152 S.W.3d 88 (Tex. Crim. App. 2004), and its progeny, indecency by contact may be subsumed as a lesser-included/incident act where the touching is part of the same continuous assaultive transaction and the State does not elect discrete acts. Here the complainant described a single uninterrupted episode in the truck cab in which the breast contact immediately preceded penetration; the State charged one date, one victim, one transaction and conceded 'we don't have multiple dates.' The error is compounded by (a) two automatic life sentences under Tex. Penal Code § 12.42(c)(2), and (b) cumulation under art. 42.08, transforming a subsumed count into a consecutive life term. Multiple-punishments double jeopardy may be raised for the first time on appeal where the violation is apparent on the face of the record (Gonzalez v. State, 8 S.W.3d 640). This is the strongest appellate issue in the record.

champion.partB: The jury assessed automatic life under Tex. Penal Code § 12.42(c)(2) on both counts and added a $10,000 fine on each. Section 12.42(c)(2) mandates 'imprisonment for life' and does not authorize a fine; a fine assessed in addition to a statutorily mandated life term is void and may be reformed or stricken on appeal or attacked as an illegal sentence at any time (Mizell v. State, 119 S.W.3d 804 (Tex. Crim. App. 2003)). The charge nonetheless authorized the jury to assess a fine alongside the mandatory life term (Excerpts 576-577, 583-586). challenger.partB: Sheikh, who disclaimed cell-site expertise (Excerpt 249) and generated State's 18 on a free consumer website, Batchgeo (Excerpts 245, 247), conceded that AT&T 'explicitly states their records and coordinates are not to be used' as accurate (Excerpt 282) and admitted the mapped Livingston arrival (9:21–9:35) conflicts with the 9:15 McDonald's video — 'That's not accurate... No.' Yet the State's 29-minute-gap venue/opportunity theory rested on this data (Excerpt 259). Flag for a reliability (Kelly/Daubert) and sufficiency analysis, and for expert-review of the raw CDRs, including the packets the detective could not identify.

challenger.quote: A. They did not. They did not follow the
challenger.partA: The detective asked the arresting police department to hold the truck and the defendant's phone when he was arrested. They never did. So the actual truck — where the State says the assault happened — and the phone were never searched or preserved as evidence.
challenger.partB: Sheikh testified that despite TCIC instructions, Spring Valley PD failed to tow the F-150 or seize the cell phone at arrest (Excerpts 237–238, 283–284), so the interior of the alleged crime-scene vehicle was never processed for corroborating or exculpatory physical evidence, and only carrier CDRs — not a phone extraction — exist. Evaluate under Youngblood/Trombetta and as a factual predicate supporting the transfer-DNA defense theory the jury never saw tested.

challenger.quote: stuff in here that's not very complimentary of my
challenger.partA: Outside the jury's presence, the prosecutor admitted that the girl's counseling records contain a lot of material that makes her look bad. Those records were never put into evidence, so the jury never saw them.
challenger.partB: On the record, the prosecutor acknowledged the Burke Center records contain material 'not very complimentary of my victim' and that 'she obviously has lots of problems,' and elected not to offer them to avoid optional completeness (Excerpt 352). The records were referenced repeatedly (10 disclosures to a therapist, medications, prior suicide attempts, mother's statements about lying and attention-seeking, Excerpts 335–338) but never admitted. Audit the completeness of the defense's copy of the Burke/therapy file and any withheld portions as Brady/Giglio impeachment of the complainant's credibility in a he-said/she-said case.

challenger.quote: item as no swabs were present inside the swab box. The
challenger.partA: One of the swabs from the hospital exam — the vulva swab — was missing from the sealed kit when the lab opened it. The box was labeled for that swab, but there was nothing inside, so it was never tested.
challenger.partB: Per the biology analyst's reading of Patnaik's notes, the vulva swab box in the SANE kit was labeled and sealed but contained no swabs, so no analysis was performed on that anatomical site. This is a chain-of-custody/evidence-integrity anomaly in the very kit the case turned on; audit hospital collection records (Schofield documented a vulva swab among the 16 swabs, Excerpt 378) against DPS intake to determine where the swab was lost and whether that discrepancy was disclosed.

challenger.quote: any kind of drugs or anything that's involved in that,
challenger.partA: The girl told several people she got dizzy and 'blacked out' after drinking something the man gave her — which suggests she may have been drugged. The nurse agreed the hospital could have drawn blood to test for drugs, but no toxicology test was ever done or produced.
challenger.partB: The complainant's account to Evan Perry (dizziness, blackout after alcohol) and her trial testimony (vision 'went white') raised an intoxication/drugging theory, yet SANE nurse Schofield confirmed blood could have been drawn and tested for drugs and no toxicology appears in State's 20 or the DPS submissions. The absence of any tox screen is both an uncollected-evidence issue and impeachment of the drugging narrative; confirm via the full CHI medical record whether any labs were drawn that night and, if so, whether results were produced.

challenger.quote: A. I never spoke with the grandmother.
challenger.partA: The detective never talked to the grandmother the girl was staying with, never went to the house where the day started, and never checked whether the fire station where she was picked up had cameras. Those witnesses and possible videos were never gathered.
challenger.partB: Sheikh conceded he never interviewed Jeri Talbot (the 'nana' present that day), never contacted the fire station near the Bentwater pickup point about cameras or witnesses (Excerpt 269), and never verified the actual route driven (Excerpt 270–271). These uninvestigated sources are referenced in testimony but absent from the disclosed file; they bear on the origin narrative (why the complainant left) and are relevant to both a Brady audit of any undisclosed patrol/canvass notes and a trial-counsel investigation review.

challenger.quote: You're not a cell phone expert, are you?
challenger.partA: The detective who made the cell phone location map admitted he is not a cell phone expert. He had only taken a couple of classes and had never testified as a cell phone expert before, but the judge still let the jury see his map and hear his conclusions about where the phone was.
challenger.partB: Sgt. Sheikh conceded on voir dire that he is not a qualified cell-site expert and has never testified as one, yet State's Exhibits 18 and 19 (his self-generated coordinate map and AT&T CDRs) were admitted over defense objections to relevance, hearsay, and the unidentified software (RR Vol. 3). Historical CSLI precision claims by lay/under-qualified witnesses are a recognized category of overstated forensic location testimony vulnerable under Tex. R. Evid. 702/Kelly and, if the underlying methodology is shown discredited or materially refined, Art. 11.073.

challenger.quote: It's a free website. It offers a free service
challenger.partA: The detective did not use professional, tested mapping tools. He typed the phone company's coordinates into a free website called Batchego to make the map the jury saw. Free consumer websites are not tested or approved for courtroom accuracy.
challenger.partB: Sheikh plotted AT&T CDR latitude/longitude values using 'Batchego.com,' a free public website with no demonstrated validation, error rate, or acceptance in the relevant scientific community. Admission of State's Ex. 18 without any Kelly/Daubert reliability showing—over preserved objection—supports a challenge to the methodology used to place the defendant's phone at specific locations and to construct the State's venue/timeline theory.

challenger.quote: and he's staying there until 9:35. That's not accurate,
challenger.partA: The detective's phone-map times did not match the McDonald's security video. The video showed the truck arriving at 9:15, but the phone data said it arrived at 9:21 and stayed until 9:35. The detective agreed his phone-location times were not accurate, yet the State still used a claimed 29-minute 'gap' from that data to argue where the assault happened.
challenger.partB: On cross, Sheikh admitted the CSLI-derived arrival window (9:21–9:35 p.m.) conflicted with the authenticated McDonald's video timestamp (9:15 p.m.), i.e., 'That's not accurate.' He also acknowledged AT&T's own records disclaim positional accuracy. The State's asserted 29-minute gap (RR3 at 183) derived from this admittedly imprecise data was the linchpin for locating the offense at FM 945/SH 156 in San Jacinto County—material both to an 11.073-type reliability challenge and to the preserved venue/directed-verdict argument.

challenger.quote: Correct. But it wasn't done by her.
challenger.partA: The DNA witness who testified did not do the actual lab work. Another analyst did the screening, and a third, unnamed analyst did the extraction and other steps. The defense objected that it could not question the people who actually handled and tested the evidence, but the judge allowed the testimony anyway.
challenger.partB: Jacaranda Solis testified as a surrogate: Patnaik performed the biology screening (Ex. 33, 35) and an unnamed analyst performed extraction/quantification/amplification; Solis performed only interpretation. Davis lodged and re-urged Confrontation objections that Solis was 'the improper witness' and that he could not cross-examine the analysts who did the testing; objections were overruled (RR3 at 33–35, 39, 57). Smith v. Arizona, 602 U.S. 779 (2024)—decided June 21, 2024, weeks after this June 3–5, 2024 trial—holds that surrogate-expert conveyance of an absent analyst's statements for their truth implicates the Confrontation Clause; the preserved objections position this claim for direct appeal in No. 09-24-00260-CR.

challenger.quote: is an updated version of one of my previous DNA reports.
challenger.partA: The DNA lab changed how it words its results in late 2023 and reissued a report in this case in May 2024 with the new wording. This shows the DNA reporting rules in this field are still changing, which can matter later if the methods change again.
challenger.partB: DPS Houston adopted a new verbal-scale/likelihood-ratio reporting standard effective November 28, 2023, and reissued the operative report (State's Ex. 37, dated 5/7/2024) superseding the 11/21/2023 report. This documented mid-case refinement of LR reporting conventions is directly relevant to Art. 11.073(d)'s 'scientific knowledge or method on which the relevant scientific evidence is based has changed' framework and should be monitored for further revisions to probabilistic-genotyping/LR reporting standards.

challenger.quote: him. I mean that's the guy.
challenger.partA: In his opening, the prosecutor told the jury the DNA numbers mean it was definitely the defendant. But DNA statistics give odds, not a certain identification, and saying 'it's him' overstates what the science can actually say.
challenger.partB: The prosecutor converted a likelihood ratio (represented as '1 in 16.8 septillion') into an unqualified source attribution—'it's him. I mean that's the guy'—in opening statement. Presenting an LR as a certainty of identity misstates the statistic (transposed-conditional/source-attribution error). Unpreserved as argument, but relevant to a cumulative overstated-identification analysis and to framing the DNA evidence's true probative limits.

challenger.quote: This is, and I'm probably not qualified to
challenger.partA: The detective admitted he was probably not qualified to explain how children's memories work, but he was still asked expert-style questions about whether kids tell the same story the same way, which supported the child witness's changing accounts.
challenger.partB: Sheikh conceded lack of qualification on child-memory science mid-answer, after which the State elicited that he had previously testified 'as an expert' on victim demeanor and absence of physical evidence, then obtained opinions normalizing inconsistencies in child disclosures (RR3 at 119–120). This is unqualified behavioral-science bolstering vulnerable under Rule 702; defense objection was lodged but the line of questioning continued.

challenger.quote: I can't compare it.
challenger.partA: The State's fingerprint examiner said he could not match the defendant's fingerprints to the old 1986 conviction papers—the very conviction that triggered an automatic life sentence. The jury found it was the same person anyway, based on ID numbers and photos rather than a fingerprint match.
challenger.partB: Investigator Goodwin admitted he could not effect a fingerprint comparison to the 1986 pen packet (State's Ex. 39) due to microfilm degradation, and could not compare the 2010 J&S right-thumbprint due to scarring; the §12.42(c)(2) automatic-life enhancement 'true' finding on both counts (sentences stacked) therefore rested on FBI/SID numbers, jail cards, photographs, and character witnesses' photo identifications. Supports a sufficiency-of-the-linkage challenge to the enhancement under Flowers v. State's totality approach, and frames the punishment verdict's dependence on non-print identifiers.

challenger.quote: I, sentence you to life in prison with a $10,000 fine.
challenger.partA: The jury found this was Mr. Ellis's second sexual offense, so Texas law required an automatic life sentence. But that specific law only allows a life sentence in prison — it does not say anything about a money fine. The jury and judge added a $10,000 fine to each count anyway. A court cannot add punishment the law does not allow, so those fines may have to be removed.
challenger.partB: The jury found the Tex. Penal Code § 12.42(c)(2) repeat-sex-offender allegation true on both counts and assessed mandatory life plus a $10,000 fine on each count, which the court pronounced. Section 12.42(c)(2) prescribes imprisonment for life only and does not authorize a fine; Texas courts have repeatedly reformed judgments to delete fines assessed alongside § 12.42(c)(2) mandatory life sentences as unauthorized. The $10,000 fine on each count is an illegal-sentence component subject to deletion by reformation, cognizable at any time under Mizell v. State, 119 S.W.3d 804 (Tex. Crim. App. 2003).

challenger.quote: fine not to exceed $10,000.00 may be imposed.
challenger.partA: The written instructions the judge read to the jury told them that, even under the automatic life sentence, they could also add a fine up to $10,000. That instruction appears to go beyond what the statute actually allows, and it invited the jury to add the unauthorized fines.
challenger.partB: The punishment charge instructed the jury that upon finding the § 12.42(c)(2) enhancement true they must assess life 'and a fine not to exceed $10,000.00 may be imposed.' This charge authorized punishment outside the statutory range, since § 12.42(c)(2) provides for life imprisonment without a fine. This supports both an Almanza charge-error claim and the illegal-sentence/reformation argument as to the fines assessed on both counts.

challenger.quote: A. I can't compare it.
challenger.partA: To trigger the automatic life sentence, the State had to prove Mr. Ellis was the same person convicted of the 1986 burglary case. Their fingerprint expert admitted he could not match the fingerprints on the old prison records to Mr. Ellis because of scarring. The State relied instead on things like an FBI number and photos. A lawyer should check whether that proof was legally enough to support the life-sentence enhancement.
challenger.partB: The State's fingerprint expert (Goodwin) conceded he could not compare the prints in State's Exhibit 39 (the 1986 burglary-with-intent-to-commit-sexual-assault pen packet, the predicate for § 12.42(c)(2) mandatory life) to the known 10-print card (38A), and likewise could not compare the thumbprint on the 2010 prohibited-weapon judgment. Identity linkage rested on FBI/SID numbers, photographs, and jail cards. While non-fingerprint identifiers can suffice under Flowers v. State, 220 S.W.3d 919 (Tex. Crim. App. 2007), counsel should evaluate a legal-sufficiency challenge to the enhancement finding, including the microfilm-degraded print card, the contested pen-packet page counts preserved by objection, and defendant's 'not true' plea.

challenger.quote: time served equals one-half of the sentence imposed, or
challenger.partA: The judge's instructions told the jury that a person becomes eligible for parole after serving half the sentence or 30 years, whichever is less. But for an automatic life sentence given to a repeat sex offender, Texas law actually requires 35 full calendar years before parole eligibility. The jury got the wrong parole information, though it may not have changed anything since the life sentence was mandatory.
challenger.partB: The punishment charge gave the standard Art. 37.07 § 4(a) parole instruction (one-half or 30 years, whichever is less), but for a life sentence imposed under § 12.42(c)(2), Tex. Gov't Code § 508.145(c) requires 35 calendar years' actual time before parole eligibility. The instruction misstated the parole law applicable to the mandatory-life scenario. No objection appears, so review would be for egregious harm under Almanza; harm is doubtful given the jury had no sentencing discretion once the enhancement was found true, but the defect should be documented.

challenger.quote: sentences run consecutively. Anything else?
challenger.partA: The judge ordered the two life sentences to be served one after the other instead of at the same time. Normally, when two charges come from the same event and one trial, sentences must run together — but Texas has an exception for sex crimes against children, which likely allows this. A lawyer should still confirm the stacking order was done correctly and is properly written in the judgment.
challenger.partB: The court granted the State's motion to cumulate and ordered the Count II life sentence consecutive to Count I. Both counts arose from a single criminal episode prosecuted in one criminal action, ordinarily requiring concurrent sentences under Tex. Penal Code § 3.03(a); however, § 3.03(b)(2)(A) authorizes cumulation for §§ 22.011 and 21.11 offenses against a victim younger than 17, which appears to apply here (complainant was 16). Counsel should verify the written cumulation order contains the specific data required by Ward/Banks (prior cause number, court, county, offense, and sentence) and matches the oral pronouncement.

challenger.quote: indecency with a child by contact is a lesser included
challenger.partA: Before the verdict, the defense lawyer argued that the touching charge (indecency) was really part of the same act as the sexual assault charge, and that punishing Mr. Ellis for both could be unfair 'double punishment.' The judge disagreed. This argument was properly raised and saved, so an appeals lawyer can look at whether two convictions and two life sentences for the same episode were allowed.
challenger.partB: Defense counsel preserved a multiple-punishments double-jeopardy/lesser-included objection to submitting both Count I (§ 22.011 penetration) and Count II (§ 21.11 indecency by breast contact), which the trial court overruled under a Blockburger analysis. Because the indecency count alleged touching of the breast — a discrete act not incident to or subsumed by the penetration under Aekins v. State, 447 S.W.3d 270 (Tex. Crim. App. 2014) — the claim likely fails, but the preserved objection and the record (single transaction, both convictions carrying stacked mandatory life terms) warrant appellate evaluation of the two-conviction, two-life-sentence outcome.
